Further Reading	1</a></p><h1><a id="_Toc228980937"></a>Section 1:  Project Overview</h1><h2><a id="_Toc228980938"></a>1.1  Introduction &amp; Vision</h2><p>The iota-dpp-app is a sophisticated, fully decentralized application (dApp) purpose-built to govern and manage Digital Product Passports (DPPs) for high-value, safety-critical manufactured components. At its core, the application functions as an immutable, on-chain ledger that chronicles the complete life history of a physical asset — from the moment superalloy raw materials are received at an investment casting foundry, all the way through active service in a jet engine, and ultimately to end-of-life decommissioning.</p><p>The primary use case demonstrated by this application is the lifecycle tracking of an Aerospace Turbine Blade. This choice is deliberate: turbine blades represent one of the most demanding engineering challenges in the world, operating under extreme thermal and mechanical loads. Their traceability, provenance, and maintenance history are not merely commercial concerns — they are direct safety imperatives governed by international aviation authorities such as the FAA (Federal Aviation Administration) and EASA (European Union Aviation Safety Agency).</p><table><tr><td><p><strong>🎯  Core Problem Statement</strong></p><p>Traditional aerospace supply chains rely on fragmented, paper-based or siloed digital records that are difficult to verify, prone to forgery, and easily lost during ownership transfers. The iota-dpp-app replaces this fragile system with a cryptographically secured, decentralized truth — where every event in a component's life is permanently anchored to the blockchain and verifiable by any authorized party.</p></td></tr></table><h2><a id="_Toc228980939"></a>1.2  Objectives</h2><ul><li>Immutability: Ensure that no historical record of a turbine blade can be altered or deleted once committed on-chain.</li><li>Transparency: Allow any stakeholder (OEMs, MRO shops, regulators, auditors) to independently verify a component's full history.</li><li>Decentralization: Eliminate single points of failure by distributing both metadata (IPFS/Filecoin) and state (IOTA EVM) across independent networks.</li><li>Digital Twin Binding: Tie the physical component to its NFT-based digital twin, ensuring the on-chain record and the physical part are inseparably linked.</li><li>Composability: Support hierarchical Bills of Materials (BOMs) by enabling sub-component NFTs that are on-chain children of parent equipment tokens.</li></ul><h2><a id="_Toc228980940"></a>1.3  Technology Stack</h2><table><thead><tr><th><p><strong>Technology / Tool</strong></p></th><th><p><strong>Role &amp; Justification</strong></p></th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><p>React 19 (TypeScript)</p></td><td><p>Primary frontend framework. TypeScript enforces strict typing across all Web3 data structures (ABIs, transaction receipts, wallet addresses), preventing runtime errors in safety-critical flows.</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>Tailwind CSS</p></td><td><p>Utility-first CSS framework enabling rapid, dark-mode optimized UI construction without custom stylesheet overhead.</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>ethers.js v6</p></td><td><p>The industry-standard JavaScript library for Ethereum-compatible blockchain interaction. Handles RPC communication, ABI encoding/decoding, transaction signing, and receipt parsing.</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>NFT.storage (IPFS + Filecoin)</p></td><td><p>Provides persistent, decentralized storage for JSON metadata. Metadata pinned to IPFS is content-addressed — the CID changes if the content changes, ensuring integrity.</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>IOTA EVM Testnet</p></td><td><p>An EVM-compatible layer on the IOTA network. Chosen for its feeless (or very low-fee) transaction model, making frequent lifecycle update transactions economically viable.</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>lucide-react</p></td><td><p>Lightweight SVG icon library for a consistent, accessible UI icon system.</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>react-hot-toast</p></td><td><p>Provides non-blocking toast notifications that elegantly communicate asynchronous transaction states (uploading, awaiting signature, mining, confirmed, error).</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>MetaMask (EIP-1193)</p></td><td><p>The browser extension wallet used for transaction signing. The app communicates with MetaMask via the EIP-1193 provider interface injected into window.ethereum.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><h2><a id="_Toc228980941"></a>1.4  Data Model &amp; Metadata Schema</h2><p>Every Digital Product Passport is represented by two inseparable layers of data: an on-chain ERC-721 NFT record stored on the IOTA EVM, and an off-chain JSON metadata object pinned to IPFS. The JSON schema is deeply structured to accommodate the full complexity of an aerospace component's lifecycle:</p><table><tr><td></td><td><p>  "name":                  "Turbine Blade #&lt;tokenId&gt;"</p><p>  "description":           "Investment Cast Aerospace Turbine Blade – Digital Product Passport on IOTA"</p><p>  "serialNumber":          "CLX-2026-&lt;tokenId&gt;"</p><p>  "manufacturer":          "Foundry ABC"</p><p>  "materialBatch":         "IN718-HEAT-45678"</p><p>  "heatNumber":            "HT-2026-089"</p><p>  "currentLifecycleStage": "ManufacturingAndInspection"</p><p>  "manufacturing":         { "processHistory": [], "ndTReports": [], "qAReports": [] }</p><p>  "supplyChain":           { "ownershipHistory": [], "vendors": {} }</p><p>  "customerLevel":         { "warrantyInfo": {}, "lifeOfPart": {} }</p><p>  "latestNotarizationHash":"0x0000...0000"</p></td></tr></table><p>A critical design principle governs all metadata updates: every mutation creates a brand-new IPFS CID, and an on-chain transaction updates the tokenURI pointer. This means the entire history of metadata changes is preserved in the immutable audit trail of blockchain transactions — even if IPFS nodes are eventually unpinned, the hashes remain on-chain as forensic evidence.</p><h2><a id="_Toc228980942"></a>1.5  Physical Asset Lifecycle Stages</h2><p>The application is architected around seven discrete lifecycle stages, each mapping precisely to a real-world supply chain checkpoint for aerospace components:</p><table><thead><tr><th><p><strong>Stage</strong></p></th><th><p><strong>Description &amp; Real-World Context</strong></p></th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><p>1. Raw Material</p></td><td><p>Superalloy ingots (e.g., Inconel 718 — a nickel-chromium alloy capable of withstanding temperatures above 700°C) are received at the foundry. Heat numbers are logged for full material traceability.</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>2. Manufacturing &amp; Inspection</p></td><td><p>The wax pattern is created, ceramic shell built, wax burned out, molten alloy poured, cooled, and the shell removed (knockout). Each step can be recorded as a distinct Process Step on-chain.</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>3. Quality Assurance</p></td><td><p>Dimensional inspection, X-ray fluoroscopy, fluorescent penetrant inspection (FPI), and other Non-Destructive Testing (NDT) methods are performed. Certificates are linked in the metadata.</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>4. Supply Chain</p></td><td><p>The blade is shipped from the foundry to the engine OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer). Ownership transfer events are recorded on-chain, providing a verifiable custody chain.</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>5. In Service</p></td><td><p>The blade is installed in a turbine engine and begins accumulating flight cycles. Cycle count and environmental exposure data can be appended to the metadata.</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>6. Maintenance</p></td><td><p>During scheduled MRO (Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul), the blade may undergo recoating, tip restoration, or thermal barrier repair. Each maintenance action is a permanent on-chain record.</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>7. End of Life</p></td><td><p>The blade is decommissioned based on life limits (flight hours or cycles), damage beyond repair limits, or regulatory mandate. On-chain decommissioning ensures the part cannot be fraudulently reintroduced into service.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><h2><a id="_Toc228980943"></a>1.6  Directory Structure &amp; Component More importantly, it illustrates the relationships between these entities — specifically which components are composed into the App root and which hooks the App delegates to for business logic.</p><table><tr><td><p><strong>📊  Class Diagram — React Components &amp; Custom Hooks</strong></p></td></tr><tr><td><p><em>Shows the attributes, methods, and relationships of all major application classes</em></p></td></tr><tr><td><p>classDiagram</p><p>    class App {</p><p>      +string tokenId</p><p>      +ModalKey activeModal</p><p>      +boolean loading</p><p>      +openModal()</p><p>      +closeModal()</p><p>      +handleConfirm()</p><p>    }</p><p>    class Header {</p><p>      +string account</p><p>      +boolean connecting</p><p>      +onConnect()</p><p>      +onDisconnect()</p><p>    }</p><p>    class ActionCard {</p><p>      +Icon icon</p><p>      +string title</p><p>      +onClick()</p><p>    }</p><p>    class Modal {</p><p>      +string title</p><p>      +Field[] fields</p><p>      +onConfirm()</p><p>      +onClose()</p><p>    }</p><p>    class useWallet {</p><p>      +string account</p><p>      +JsonRpcSigner signer</p><p>      +connect()</p><p>      +disconnect()</p><p>    }</p><p>    class useContract {</p><p>      +mintEquipment()</p><p>      +mintPart()</p><p>      +updateMetadata()</p><p>      +recordProcessStep()</p><p>    }</p><p>    App *-- Header</p><p>    App *-- ActionCard</p><p>    App *-- Modal</p><p>    App ..&gt; useWallet : uses</p><p>    App ..&gt; useContract : uses</p></td></tr></table><p><img src="data:image/png;base64," /></p><p>Key Relationships Explained:</p><ul><li><strong>Composition (App *-- Header / ActionCard / Modal): </strong>The App component directly owns and renders these child components. When App unmounts, these children are destroyed. This models the React parent-child rendering tree.</li><li><strong>Dependency (App ..&gt; useWallet / useContract): </strong>App depends on these hooks at runtime but does not "own" them in the OOP sense. The hooks manage their own internal state via React's useState and useEffect primitives.</li><li><strong>useWallet provides the signer to useContract: </strong>The JsonRpcSigner object obtained from MetaMask (via useWallet) is passed to useContract, allowing it to sign and broadcast transactions. This is the critical authentication handshake between the UI and the blockchain.</li></ul><table><tr><td><p><strong>💡  Design Pattern Note</strong></p><p>The architecture follows the Custom Hooks pattern popularized in React 16.8+. By separating Web3 state management into useWallet and useContract, the codebase achieves a clean separation of concerns — UI components remain stateless and testable, while all blockchain complexity is contained in hooks.</p></td></tr></table><h2><a id="_Toc228980946"></a>2.2  Component Diagram — System Boundaries &amp; Interfaces</h2><p>Purpose: While the class diagram focuses on code-level detail, the component diagram zooms out to show how the high-level system components interact through defined interfaces. This is critical for understanding the architectural boundaries between what runs in the user's browser (the React SPA) and what is accessed over the network (decentralized infrastructure).</p><table><tr><td><p><strong>📊  Component Diagram — Frontend App vs External Networks</strong></p></td></tr><tr><td><p><em>Illustrates system boundaries between the React frontend, IPFS, and the IOTA blockchain</em></p></td></tr><tr><td><p>flowchart TB</p><p>    subgraph Frontend ["Frontend Application (Browser)"]</p><p>        UI["UI Components (React)"]</p><p>        Hooks["Business Logic (Hooks)"]</p><p>    end</p><p>    subgraph External ["External Decentralized Networks"]</p><p>        IPFS["NFT.storage / IPFS"]</p><p>        IOTA["IOTA EVM Smart Contract"]</p><p>    end</p><p>    UI --&gt;|"Calls Functions"| Hooks</p><p>    Hooks --&gt;|"Uploads JSON via HTTPS POST"| IPFS</p><p>    Hooks --&gt;|"Sends Transactions via Ethers.js"| IOTA</p></td></tr></table><p><img src="data:image/png;base64," /></p><p>Component Interaction Analysis:</p><ul><li><strong>UI Components → Hooks: </strong>The React component tree makes function calls (e.g., mintEquipment(tokenId)) to the hook layer. React's prop drilling or context passing is used to thread hook functions down to the appropriate UI elements.</li><li><strong>Hooks → IPFS (NFT.storage): </strong>Before any blockchain transaction is dispatched, the hook serializes the current metadata JSON object and makes a standard HTTPS POST request to the NFT.storage REST API. The response is a CID (Content Identifier) — a cryptographic hash of the data that serves as the permanent address of that metadata on the IPFS network.</li><li><strong>Hooks → IOTA EVM: </strong>Armed with the CID, the hook constructs an ethers.js transaction targeting the deployed Solidity smart contract. This transaction is sent to the IOTA EVM node via JSON-RPC, requesting MetaMask to sign it first.</li></ul><table><tr><td><p><strong>🔗  Why Two External Networks?</strong></p><p>Storing metadata entirely on-chain would be prohibitively expensive and technically infeasible for large JSON objects. The IPFS-on-chain-pointer pattern (sometimes called 'lazy loading' for NFTs) stores only the immutable CID on-chain (cheap, permanent) while the full metadata lives on IPFS (cheap, content-addressed). The IOTA EVM's low-fee architecture further reduces the economic barrier of frequent metadata updates.</p></td></tr></table><h2><a id="_Toc228980947"></a>2.3  Deployment Diagram — Infrastructure Topology</h2><p>Purpose: The deployment diagram maps software artifacts to the physical or virtual infrastructure nodes they run on. For a Web3 dApp, this is especially important because the 'backend' is not a traditional server — it is a globally distributed blockchain network and a content-addressed peer-to-peer storage network.</p><table><tr><td><p><strong>📊  Deployment Diagram — Infrastructure Nodes &amp; Communication Protocols</strong></p></td></tr><tr><td><p><em>Maps all software components to their respective infrastructure environments</em></p></td></tr><tr><td><p>flowchart TD</p><p>    subgraph UserEnvironment ["User Environment (Client Device)"]</p><p>        Browser["Web Browser — React SPA (JavaScript Bundle)"]</p><p>        MetaMask["MetaMask Browser Extension (Key Manager)"]</p><p>    end</p><p>    subgraph WebServer ["Hosting Layer"]</p><p>        CDN["Static Web Host — Vercel / Netlify (CDN-distributed)"]</p><p>    end</p><p>    subgraph DecentralizedNetworks ["Decentralized Infrastructure"]</p><p>        IOTA_RPC["IOTA EVM RPC Node (JSON-RPC over HTTPS)"]</p><p>        IPFS_Node["IPFS / Filecoin Node (NFT.storage REST API)"]</p><p>    end</p><p>    Browser --&gt;|"HTTPS: Fetches JS/CSS/HTML Assets"| CDN</p><p>    Browser &lt;--&gt;|"EIP-1193: window.ethereum API"| MetaMask</p><p>    MetaMask &lt;--&gt;|"JSON-RPC: eth_sendTransaction, eth_call"| IOTA_RPC</p><p>    Browser --&gt;|"HTTPS REST API: storeBlob(JSON)"| IPFS_Node</p></td></tr></table><p><img src="data:image/png;base64," /></p><p>Infrastructure Node Breakdown:</p><ul><li><strong>Web Browser (React SPA): </strong>The entire application runs client-side. There is no traditional application server. The JavaScript bundle (compiled TypeScript) is downloaded once from the CDN and executes entirely in the browser's V8 engine.</li><li><strong>MetaMask Extension: </strong>Acts as a secure hardware-separated key management layer. Private keys never leave MetaMask — the extension signs transaction payloads locally and sends only the signed transaction to the RPC node.</li><li><strong>Static Web Host (Vercel/Netlify): </strong>Hosts the compiled React build artifacts (HTML, CSS, JS chunks). A CDN distributes these assets globally, minimizing load time. No server-side logic is required — this dramatically reduces hosting costs and attack surface.</li><li><strong>IOTA EVM RPC Node: </strong>The gateway to the IOTA blockchain network. The application sends JSON-RPC method calls (eth_sendRawTransaction, eth_call, eth_getTransactionReceipt) to this node to read and write blockchain state.</li><li><strong>IPFS / Filecoin Node: </strong>NFT.storage provides an enterprise-grade API that pins uploaded data to both the IPFS network and Filecoin for long-term persistence. Once pinned, the content is addressable by its CID from any IPFS node globally.</li></ul><h2><a id="_Toc228980948"></a>2.4  Object Diagram — NFT Instance in Memory</h2><p>Purpose: The object diagram depicts specific instances of classes at a particular point in time. This is invaluable for developers who need to understand the concrete shape of runtime data before writing code that consumes it.</p><table><tr><td><p><strong>📊  Object Diagram — Turbine Blade Token #1 Instance</strong></p></td></tr><tr><td><p><em>Depicts a concrete NFT instance and its resolved IPFS metadata at runtime</em></p></td></tr><tr><td><p>classDiagram</p><p>    class TurbineBlade_Token1 {</p><p>        &lt;&lt;NFT Instance — IOTA EVM&gt;&gt;</p><p>        tokenId:  1</p><p>        owner:    "0xAbC...def123"</p><p>        tokenURI: "ipfs://bafyreighf3..."</p><p>    }</p><p>    class Metadata_IPFS_bafyreigh {</p><p>        &lt;&lt;JSON Object — IPFS&gt;&gt;</p><p>        name:                 "Turbine Blade #1"</p><p>        serialNumber:         "CLX-2026-1"</p><p>        manufacturer:         "Foundry ABC"</p><p>        heatNumber:           "HT-2026-089"</p><p>        currentLifecycleStage:"ManufacturingAndInspection"</p><p>        materialBatch:        "IN718-HEAT-45678"</p><p>        lastUpdated:          "2026-05-06T10:00:00.000Z"</p><p>    }</p><p>    TurbineBlade_Token1 --&gt; Metadata_IPFS_bafyreigh : tokenURI resolves to</p></td></tr></table><p><img src="data:image/png;base64," /><br /></p><p>Reading the Object Diagram:</p><ul><li><strong>TurbineBlade_Token1 (on-chain): </strong>This represents the ERC-721 token slot in the Solidity smart contract's storage. The tokenURI is a pointer to the IPFS CID.</li><li><strong>Metadata_IPFS_bafyreigh (off-chain): </strong>This represents the actual JSON document stored on IPFS. Replacing IPFS or the blockchain network only requires changes to this layer.</li><li><strong>External Systems: </strong>The Smart Contract, NFT.storage, and MetaMask are all external to the application’s codebase. They are out of the development team’s direct control — changes to their APIs or behavior can break the application, making them important risk considerations.</li></ul><h2><a id="_Toc228980959"></a>2.15  Architecture Pattern — Fat Client / dApp Model</h2><p>Purpose: This diagram explicitly labels and illustrates the overarching architectural pattern of the application: the Fat Client dApp architecture. Understanding this pattern is essential for architects evaluating the system’s non-functional characteristics: security model, availability guarantees, and scalability profile.</p><table><tr><td><p><strong>📊  Architecture Pattern — Fat Client / Decentralized Backend</strong></p></td></tr><tr><td><p><em>Contrasts the client-heavy dApp pattern with traditional client-server architecture</em></p></td></tr><tr><td><p>flowchart LR</p><p>    subgraph FatClient [“CLIENT LAYER (Fat Client — Runs in Browser)”]</p><p>        React[“React UI</p><p>(Presentation Logic)”]</p><p>        Ethers[“Ethers.js v6</p><p>(Web3 Adapter)”]</p><p>        NFTClient[“NFT.storage Client</p><p>(IPFS Adapter)”]</p><p>        TypeScript[“TypeScript</p><p>(Type Safety)”]</p><p>    end</p><p>    subgraph DecentralizedBackend [“DECENTRALIZED BACKEND (No Traditional Server)”]</p><p>        EVM[“IOTA EVM</p><p>(Smart Contract State)”]</p><p>        IPFS[“IPFS Network</p><p>(Metadata Storage)”]</p><p>        Filecoin[“Filecoin</p><p>(Persistence Guarantees)”]</p><p>    end</p><p>    React --&gt; Ethers</p><p>    React --&gt; NFTClient</p><p>    Ethers &lt;--&gt;|"JSON-RPC over HTTPS"| EVM</p><p>    NFTClient --&gt;|"REST API over HTTPS"| IPFS</p><p>    IPFS -.-&gt;|"Pinned for persistence"| Filecoin</p></td></tr></table><p><img src="data:image/png;base64," /></p><p>Pattern Trade-off Analysis:</p><table><thead><tr><th><p><strong>Characteristic</strong></p></th><th><p><strong>Fat Client dApp vs Traditional Client-Server</strong></p></th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><p>Business Logic Location</p></td><td><p>Fat Client: All logic runs in the browser. Traditional: Logic runs on the server.</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>Authentication</p></td><td><p>Fat Client: Cryptographic key-based (wallet signature). Traditional: Username/password or OAuth tokens.</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>Data Persistence</p></td><td><p>Fat Client: Smart contract state (immutable) + IPFS (content-addressed). Traditional: Mutable database (SQL/NoSQL).</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>Availability</p></td><td><p>Fat Client: Depends on blockchain and IPFS uptime (high, decentralized). Traditional: Depends on server/database uptime (single point of failure).</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>Scalability</p></td><td><p>Fat Client: Blockchain throughput is the bottleneck (limited TPS). Traditional: Horizontal server scaling is easier.</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>Auditability</p></td><td><p>Fat Client: Every state change is publicly verifiable on-chain. Traditional: Audit logs are mutable and admin-controlled.</p></td></tr><tr><td><p>Hosting Cost</p></td><td><p>Fat Client: Static file hosting only (very cheap). Traditional: Application servers, load balancers, databases (expensive).</p></td></tr></tbody></table><h1><a id="_Toc228980960"></a>Section 3:  Scope of Project</h1><h2><a id="_Toc228980961"></a>3.1  Current Scope — What Is Built</h2><p>The current version of the iota-dpp-app delivers a fully functional proof-of-concept that demonstrates the viability of blockchain-based Digital Product Passports for aerospace components. History is not displayed in the UI.</li><li>NFT.storage payment management: The NFT.storage API key is a placeholder. By combining the IOTA EVM's low-fee transaction model with IPFS's content-addressed decentralized storage, the application achieves a level of data integrity and transparency that is fundamentally impossible with traditional centralized systems.</p><p>The architectural decisions made in the application — the Fat Client dApp model, the separation of on-chain state from off-chain metadata, the custom hooks pattern for Web3 logic isolation, and the seven-stage lifecycle state machine — are well-reasoned and scalable. They provide a solid foundation upon which the production enhancements described in Section 4 can be built incrementally.</p><p>The most critical next steps for production readiness are: (1) smart contract RBAC implementation to enforce authorization, (2) on-chain lifecycle state enforcement to prevent fraudulent transitions, and (3) the development of a full history indexing and display system to unlock the full value of the immutable on-chain audit trail.</p><table><tr><td><p><strong>🚀  Strategic Value Proposition</strong></p><p>In an industry where a single counterfeit or improperly maintained turbine blade can cause catastrophic loss of life, the immutability and verifiability guarantees of a blockchain-based DPP system are not just technically interesting — they are a genuine safety imperative.
